1dkrkrd:181: From a technical implementation standpoint, code-review-graph's core is parsing code into an AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) rather than just doing text indexing. Tree-sitter, as a parser generator, can accurately identify the boundaries of code entities such as function definitions, function calls, classes, and import statements, and turn them into nodes and edges in the graph. This structured relationship representation makes queries like "who calls this function" and "which files reference this class" possible, instead of relying on fuzzy keyword matching.

1kcqjaw:187: From a broader perspective, code-review-graph represents a paradigm shift for AI coding tools: from "the model temporarily understands code" to "the model queries structured code memory." This is fundamentally different from traditional RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)—instead of stuffing document fragments into the context, the model can actively traverse and query the relationship graph of code. When this capability is combined with the MCP protocol, the next step for AI coding is not just making the model stronger, but giving it continuously accumulating project-level understanding.

e6wb9y:363: Have you ever run into this situation: in Claude Code, you ask "How does this auth flow work?", "What will be affected if I change this class?", or "Help me review the recent changes", and it starts searching, reading, and assembling context over and over again. In small projects, this approach isn't a big deal. There are few files, call chains are simple, and the AI can piece together an answer after a few rounds of ad-hoc reading. But as soon as the project becomes a monorepo, or the backend services start splitting into multiple modules, the cost of the AI re-understanding context each time becomes painfully obvious. Over time, you'll notice a very real problem: AI's understanding of the codebase is hard to accumulate continuously.

Traditional code review relies on manual judgment or full scans, while blast-radius analysis can trace call chains and dependency chains, locate relevant test files, and output the minimal necessary review context. This "narrow the scope first, then make judgments" approach is highly consistent with how human engineers handle complex code changes.
